Echipajele medicale le-au diagnosticat cu etilism acut şi le-au transportat la spital. Părinţii fetelor au primit câte o amendă de 500 de lei.

romania.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

medical.title: Psilocybin may improve a difficult-to-treat symptom of depression, study finds
medical.summary: New research from the University of Colorado Anschutz suggests that psilocybin may help improve anhedonia, the loss of interest or ability to experience pleasure, in people with treatment-resistant depression. In a clinical trial, researchers found significant improvement in this difficult-to-treat symptom eight weeks after treatment, offering new insight into psilocybin's potential role in depression care.

medical.title: Understanding epilepsy and seizures: Q&A with epileptologist
medical.summary: Epilepsy, a chronic neurological condition of the central nervous system, affects millions of people, with overactive or misfiring electrical signals in the brain leading to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.

medical.title: New review protocol outlines plan to evaluate quit-smoking support for ADHD and autism
medical.summary: Published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the protocol "Smoking cessation interventions in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD)" was developed by the South East Smokefree Alliance in collaboration with academics at the University of Bristol.

medical.title: Nearly 1 in 10 US adults report having chronic hand eczema
medical.summary: Chronic hand eczema (CHE) is common, impacting nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

medical.title: FDA approves new drug for advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
medical.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Janssen Biotech's Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed during or after receipt of platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

medical.title: Defibrillator drones could arrive ahead of ambulances in hundreds of cardiac arrest cases
medical.summary: Drones carrying defibrillators could arrive ahead of ambulances at hundreds of cardiac arrest incidents each year, potentially creating opportunities for earlier treatment, according to new research. The study, published in the journal Reliability Engineering & System Safety, also found they could improve emergency response coverage in parts of Scotland.

medical.title: Beer, but not wine, linked to higher risk of kidney injury
medical.summary: Regular drinkers of beer or spirits may face a significantly greater risk of acute kidney injury, according to a new study that analyzed data from more than 250,000 U.K. adults. However, the same association was not found for wine drinkers.

medical.title: Vest that maps heart's electrical activity could flag health risks
medical.summary: A vest that reads the heart's electrical signals could detect older people with risky age-related changes in their hearts, according to a study presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions conference held in Chicago Nov. 6–9.

medical.title: Large and very small waist sizes linked to heightened death risk across weight range
medical.summary: Both large and very small waist sizes are linked to a heightened risk of death across a broad range of body weights, finds a large study of more than 17 million adults, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

medical.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to inadequate intake of key nutrients in some people
medical.summary: Drugs taken to suppress appetite, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, are associated with inadequate intakes of key nutrients and energy in some people, finds a small exploratory study published in the journal BMJ Nutrition Prevention & Health.

medical.title: Many claims for health tests marketed to UK consumers are unsubstantiated
medical.summary: Many of the claims made for the benefits of health tests marketed to U.K. consumers are unsubstantiated, with little information provided on their potential harms and limitations, finds an assessment of the websites of 50 commercial test vendors, published in the journal BMJ Open.

medical.title: First evidence from a Chinese population supports review of long-term blood monitoring for local clozapine use
medical.summary: An international research team led by the Department of Psychiatry, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), has completed a long-term population-based research study to improve care for people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), the most severe form of this mental health condition. The findings reinforce the importance of timely access to clozapine and provide the first large-scale evidence from a Chinese population to support a review of Hong Kong's long-term blood monitoring requirements.

medical.title: Implanted electrodes restore function after severe muscle loss in early tests
medical.summary: Traumatic muscle injuries, whether from battlefield wounds, gunshots, surgical resections, or major open fractures, can cause volumetric muscle loss (VML), the loss of so much tissue that the muscle cannot regenerate on its own. Recovery typically brings chronic inflammation, scarring, and permanent weakness. Current treatments remain palliative, with none reliably restoring the lost muscle.

medical.title: Chronic loneliness increases dementia risk by 38%, but occasional loneliness appears harmless, 30-year study finds
medical.summary: A new study that tracked people over the course of 30 years finds that only chronic, persistent loneliness is strongly linked with dementia.

medical.title: Forgetful neural networks could shed light on how humans learn
medical.summary: How the brain learns is one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in science. Researchers in artificial intelligence from the University of Groningen (the Netherlands) and KU Leuven (Belgium) hope that a specific type of forgetting in artificial neural networks will help to capture what is happening in the human brain. The study is published in the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

medical.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
medical.summary: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

medical.title: Regenerated bone keeps maturing after its shape is largely restored, study reveals
medical.summary: Regeneration is often judged by what researchers can see—whether missing tissue has returned and its shape has been restored. But a new Texas A&M study shows that bone may continue to mature mechanically beneath the surface even after it appears whole.

medical.title: Your gut bacteria help your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
medical.summary: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

medical.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
medical.summary: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

medical.title: Novel algorithm predicts brain surgery outcomes in dystonia patients
medical.summary: Less than 5% of patients with dystonia—a debilitating neurological movement disorder—undergo deep brain stimulation (DBS) treatment, even though it is one of the few interventions that directly target the abnormal brain processes underlying the condition. The surgical treatment is highly underutilized, likely due to its invasiveness and the lack of objective markers of who may benefit. Even among those who undergo surgery, outcomes vary widely, depending on patient characteristics and external influences.

science.title: New research finds AI adoption is associated with more managers—and different managerial skills
science.summary: A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements.

science.title: Invasive plants show limited spread in Andalusia's mountains
science.summary: A study by the University of Córdoba (UCO) departments of Forest Engineering and of Botany, Ecology and Plant Physiology reveals that the presence of invasive plants in Sierra Nevada and the Sierra de los Filabres—two mountain ecosystems in Andalusia that are especially vulnerable to climate change and home to unique plant species—is currently low. Specifically, invasive plants are most common in the areas closest to the edges of roads, and their presence declines at the highest points of the mountains.

science.title: Gender differences in values are not widening in Europe after all
science.summary: In recent years, public discussion has focused on the increasingly conservative values of young men. A recently published study indicates that this is primarily a phenomenon prominent in social and conventional media, not an overall trend.

science.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
science.summary: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even.

science.title: Writing as it should be or as it sounds: Reconstructing how Old English disappeared
science.summary: In the twelfth century, the English-speaking world underwent a major change: Old English gave way to Middle English. In his dissertation, Ph.D. candidate Amos van Baalen uses sermons to reconstruct how this change took place.

science.title: How much CO₂ will stay? New study estimates long-term residual emissions under the EU Emissions Trading System
science.summary: Current CO₂ emissions covered by the EU Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS1) could be substantially reduced by 2040. A new study by the Oeko-Institut, commissioned by Carbon Market Watch, examines the level of emissions that could remain in 2040 and 2050. In 2040, installations covered by the EU-ETS1—including waste incineration—could still emit between 159 and 231 million metric tons of CO₂.

science.title: How do human lifestyles affect the gut microbiome of our canine companions?
science.summary: Dogs have been living side by side with humans for millennia, but a new study underscores how much we have yet to learn about man's best friend. The study, which looked at hundreds of dogs across four nations, found that the lifestyles of pet owners appear to play a significant role in determining what constitutes a healthy gut microbiome for their dog companions.

science.title: How machine learning can tackle lead pipe challenges
science.summary: A new machine learning tool developed through the Centre for Resilience in Environment, Water and Waste (CREWW) could help water companies identify properties most likely to be connected to lead service pipes.

science.title: Study tracks what students learn from online teamwork and fieldwork abroad
science.summary: Can a solution that cuts food waste in Tokyo work in Seoul too? Exploring a familiar problem with peers abroad can help students question what they take for granted at home and see how their knowledge might apply to real-world sustainability challenges. As educators put time and care into designing international courses, what do students take away from the experience, and what stays with them after the course ends?

science.title: Quantum-gas microscope resolves the 'color' of individual atoms in a single shot
science.summary: In 2024, researchers at the Ultracold Quantum Gases group at ICFO built a quantum-gas microscope capable of imaging individual atoms in strontium quantum gases for the first time, marking a key enabling step for quantum simulation. At that time, the researchers imaged strontium-84, a boson that has no spin.

science.title: The 12th‑century Chinese poet who was among the first to explore the inner lives of cats
science.summary: If you're reading this, then your media feed, like mine, is probably full of cats.

science.title: More than meets the eye: Refugee reception in eastern Germany can vary by group composition
science.summary: Imagine a group of newcomers in your local area. Would you expect your neighbors to welcome them or react with reluctance? Would it make a difference how many men and women were in the group, or whether they appeared white or nonwhite?

science.title: The Gulf's oil-eating microbes lay in wait before Deepwater Horizon spill, frozen samples suggest
science.summary: A year before the Deepwater Horizon spill, a NOAA crew scooped up seawater from the Gulf and froze it. Sixteen years later, FIU biologist Shen Jean Lim tested it only to discover the microbes that devoured much of the oil in 2010 were nowhere to be found in 2009. So where did they come from?

science.title: Lasers near physical limits of miniaturization open possibilities for tracking life at the nanoscale
science.summary: From tracking how cancer develops to exploring how the brain works, scientists need ways to observe biological processes at increasingly smaller scales. Beyond tracking how cells move and interact, researchers need to understand how tiny structures within cells, including organelles and molecular complexes, behave and change over time. However, identifying and tracking these microscopic targets individually remains a major challenge.

science.title: New model identifies priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile
science.summary: Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

science.title: New daisy genus named after botanist
science.summary: Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) botanist professor Pieter Pelser has been recognized with one of the highest honors in taxonomy, with a newly established South American daisy genus named Pelseria in acknowledgment of his decades-long contribution to studying the family tree of plants.

science.title: New Asian flying frog species identified in Indonesia
science.summary: In the lush mountain rainforests of Indonesia, researchers have identified a new species of Asian flying frog with distinctive physical features, calls and unusual egg-laying habits. The discovery is described in a paper published in the journal Zootaxa by scientists from Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense in Indonesia, the University of California, Davis, and other collaborators.

science.title: Extreme cold preserves passion fruit's vitamin C, but not all of its antioxidants
science.summary: Passion fruit can travel thousands of kilometers before it reaches international markets. Along the way, one of the food industry's biggest challenges is making sure its nutritional qualities survive processing, storage and transport.

science.title: Optimized supercomputer workflow accelerates protein-structure prediction
science.summary: A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)-led team has harnessed the power of El Capitan to accelerate generation of predicted protein structures, drastically reducing the computing time required and opening new possibilities for drug discovery, biological research and national security applications.

science.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
science.summary: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write […]

science.title: Repurposed battery molecules drive key chemical reactions where oil meets water
science.summary: The process of producing essential medicines and fine chemicals has long been powered by reactions involving intense heat, heavy-metal catalysts and hazardous hydrogen gas. Now, a team of Harvard chemists and engineers has demonstrated that these critical transformations can be driven cleanly by electricity, right at the boundary where oil and water meet.

science.title: Two proteins key to cellulose synthase trafficking and cell wall formation identified
science.summary: A new study has identified Arabidopsis SNARE proteins VAMP726 and VAMP725 as key components of the trafficking of cellulose synthase (CESA), helping support the formation of both primary and secondary cell walls.

science.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
science.summary: On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% […]

science.title: New platform improves accuracy of molecular counting in RNA-sequencing
science.summary: The open-source platform, called UMIche (pronounced "you-me-kay"), is described in a new study published in Nature Communications. It addresses a common challenge in RNA-sequencing, where errors during sequencing can lead to inaccurate measurements of gene expression.

environment.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
environment.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

environment.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
environment.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

environment.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

După ce a inundat pagina de Facebook a Ministerul Sănătății cu poze și clipuri cu el în diverse ipostaze care de care mai imbecile, ministrul Dorel Rogobete a plusat și a cerut și pagină de OnlyFans pentru minister. „Domnul ministru Rogobete ne-a spus că vrea să pună și poze mai deocheate […] The post Ministerul Sănătății și-a făcut cont pe OnlyFans, că vrea Rogobete să posteze poze cu el și acolo appeared first on Times New Roman .

mix_items.summary: Moșul vine o dată pe an, dar magia adevărată începe atunci când alegem să fim alături de copii și în celelalte 364 de zile. Anul acesta, EduAct lansează o campanie de Crăciun cu o misiune dublă: să aducă daruri sub brad pentru peste 250 de copii din comunități vulnerabile educațional din județul Călărași și să […] Articolul Peste 250 de motive să fim ajutoarele Moșului. mix_items.title: Trei eleve din Neamț au ajuns la spital, după ce au mers bete la școală și li s-a făcut rău. Ce amendă au primit părinții
mix_items.summary: Două fete în vârstă de 15 ani şi una de 16 ani, toate din judeţul Neamţ, au băut o sticlă de vodcă înainte de a merge la şcoală, iar când au ajuns la unitatea de învăţământ li s-a făcut rău şi au sunat la 112. Echipajele medicale le-au diagnosticat cu etilism acut şi le-au transportat la spital. Părinţii fetelor au primit câte o amendă de 500 de lei.

mix_items.summary: Fundația Motivation România se numără printre organizațiile care au contribuit la dezvoltarea Responsible Wheelchair Donation Toolkit, un ghid realizat de International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP), care promovează practici responsabile și sustenabile în donarea de scaune rulante, la nivel internațional. Cristian Ispas, membru fondator al Fundației Motivation România, a participat la discuțiile grupului de lucru,... mix_items.summary: Ghid antibullying cu activități testate de mii de copii și 43 de ONG-uri. Articolul “Școala în care ne simțim bine” apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.summary: “Start în educație” în anul școlar 2026-2027: 5 milioane de euro pentru îmbunătățirea accesului la educație timpurie de calitate pentru... mix_items.summary: București, 30 octombrie. Fundația World Vision România solicită Camerei Deputaților, în calitate de for decizional, să adopte proiectul de lege... mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Psilocybin may improve a difficult-to-treat symptom of depression, study finds
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of Colorado Anschutz suggests that psilocybin may help improve anhedonia, the loss of interest or ability to experience pleasure, in people with treatment-resistant depression. In a clinical trial, researchers found significant improvement in this difficult-to-treat symptom eight weeks after treatment, offering new insight into psilocybin's potential role in depression care.

mix_items.title: New research finds AI adoption is associated with more managers—and different managerial skills
mix_items.summary: A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements.

mix_items.title: Understanding epilepsy and seizures: Q&A with epileptologist
mix_items.summary: Epilepsy, a chronic neurological condition of the central nervous system, affects millions of people, with overactive or misfiring electrical signals in the brain leading to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.

mix_items.title: Invasive plants show limited spread in Andalusia's mountains
mix_items.summary: A study by the University of Córdoba (UCO) departments of Forest Engineering and of Botany, Ecology and Plant Physiology reveals that the presence of invasive plants in Sierra Nevada and the Sierra de los Filabres—two mountain ecosystems in Andalusia that are especially vulnerable to climate change and home to unique plant species—is currently low. Specifically, invasive plants are most common in the areas closest to the edges of roads, and their presence declines at the highest points of the mountains.

mix_items.title: New review protocol outlines plan to evaluate quit-smoking support for ADHD and autism
mix_items.summary: Published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, the protocol "Smoking cessation interventions in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD)" was developed by the South East Smokefree Alliance in collaboration with academics at the University of Bristol.

mix_items.title: Gender differences in values are not widening in Europe after all
mix_items.summary: In recent years, public discussion has focused on the increasingly conservative values of young men. A recently published study indicates that this is primarily a phenomenon prominent in social and conventional media, not an overall trend.

mix_items.title: Nearly 1 in 10 US adults report having chronic hand eczema
mix_items.summary: Chronic hand eczema (CHE) is common, impacting nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

mix_items.title: FDA approves new drug for advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Janssen Biotech's Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed during or after receipt of platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: How restaurants can make sustainable dining choices easier while still making a profit
mix_items.summary: Canadians are eating out less. A 2025 survey found 57% of them are cooking at home more often to save money, while 69% of restaurant operators say customers are dining out less because of affordability. According to Restaurants Canada, 41% of operators are either losing money or breaking even.

mix_items.title: Writing as it should be or as it sounds: Reconstructing how Old English disappeared
mix_items.summary: In the twelfth century, the English-speaking world underwent a major change: Old English gave way to Middle English. In his dissertation, Ph.D. candidate Amos van Baalen uses sermons to reconstruct how this change took place.

mix_items.title: How much CO₂ will stay? New study estimates long-term residual emissions under the EU Emissions Trading System
mix_items.summary: Current CO₂ emissions covered by the EU Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS1) could be substantially reduced by 2040. A new study by the Oeko-Institut, commissioned by Carbon Market Watch, examines the level of emissions that could remain in 2040 and 2050. In 2040, installations covered by the EU-ETS1—including waste incineration—could still emit between 159 and 231 million metric tons of CO₂.

mix_items.title: Defibrillator drones could arrive ahead of ambulances in hundreds of cardiac arrest cases
mix_items.summary: Drones carrying defibrillators could arrive ahead of ambulances at hundreds of cardiac arrest incidents each year, potentially creating opportunities for earlier treatment, according to new research. The study, published in the journal Reliability Engineering & System Safety, also found they could improve emergency response coverage in parts of Scotland.

mix_items.title: How do human lifestyles affect the gut microbiome of our canine companions?
mix_items.summary: Dogs have been living side by side with humans for millennia, but a new study underscores how much we have yet to learn about man's best friend. The study, which looked at hundreds of dogs across four nations, found that the lifestyles of pet owners appear to play a significant role in determining what constitutes a healthy gut microbiome for their dog companions.

mix_items.title: How machine learning can tackle lead pipe challenges
mix_items.summary: A new machine learning tool developed through the Centre for Resilience in Environment, Water and Waste (CREWW) could help water companies identify properties most likely to be connected to lead service pipes.

mix_items.title: Beer, but not wine, linked to higher risk of kidney injury
mix_items.summary: Regular drinkers of beer or spirits may face a significantly greater risk of acute kidney injury, according to a new study that analyzed data from more than 250,000 U.K. adults. However, the same association was not found for wine drinkers.

mix_items.title: Vest that maps heart's electrical activity could flag health risks
mix_items.summary: A vest that reads the heart's electrical signals could detect older people with risky age-related changes in their hearts, according to a study presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions conference held in Chicago Nov. 6–9.

mix_items.title: Study tracks what students learn from online teamwork and fieldwork abroad
mix_items.summary: Can a solution that cuts food waste in Tokyo work in Seoul too? Exploring a familiar problem with peers abroad can help students question what they take for granted at home and see how their knowledge might apply to real-world sustainability challenges. As educators put time and care into designing international courses, what do students take away from the experience, and what stays with them after the course ends?

mix_items.title: Quantum-gas microscope resolves the 'color' of individual atoms in a single shot
mix_items.summary: In 2024, researchers at the Ultracold Quantum Gases group at ICFO built a quantum-gas microscope capable of imaging individual atoms in strontium quantum gases for the first time, marking a key enabling step for quantum simulation. At that time, the researchers imaged strontium-84, a boson that has no spin.

mix_items.title: The 12th‑century Chinese poet who was among the first to explore the inner lives of cats
mix_items.summary: If you're reading this, then your media feed, like mine, is probably full of cats.

mix_items.title: Large and very small waist sizes linked to heightened death risk across weight range
mix_items.summary: Both large and very small waist sizes are linked to a heightened risk of death across a broad range of body weights, finds a large study of more than 17 million adults, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

mix_items.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to inadequate intake of key nutrients in some people
mix_items.summary: Drugs taken to suppress appetite, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, are associated with inadequate intakes of key nutrients and energy in some people, finds a small exploratory study published in the journal BMJ Nutrition Prevention & Health.

mix_items.title: Many claims for health tests marketed to UK consumers are unsubstantiated
mix_items.summary: Many of the claims made for the benefits of health tests marketed to U.K. consumers are unsubstantiated, with little information provided on their potential harms and limitations, finds an assessment of the websites of 50 commercial test vendors, published in the journal BMJ Open.

mix_items.title: First evidence from a Chinese population supports review of long-term blood monitoring for local clozapine use
mix_items.summary: An international research team led by the Department of Psychiatry, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), has completed a long-term population-based research study to improve care for people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS), the most severe form of this mental health condition. The findings reinforce the importance of timely access to clozapine and provide the first large-scale evidence from a Chinese population to support a review of Hong Kong's long-term blood monitoring requirements.

mix_items.title: More than meets the eye: Refugee reception in eastern Germany can vary by group composition
mix_items.summary: Imagine a group of newcomers in your local area. Would you expect your neighbors to welcome them or react with reluctance? Would it make a difference how many men and women were in the group, or whether they appeared white or nonwhite?

mix_items.title: Implanted electrodes restore function after severe muscle loss in early tests
mix_items.summary: Traumatic muscle injuries, whether from battlefield wounds, gunshots, surgical resections, or major open fractures, can cause volumetric muscle loss (VML), the loss of so much tissue that the muscle cannot regenerate on its own. Recovery typically brings chronic inflammation, scarring, and permanent weakness. Current treatments remain palliative, with none reliably restoring the lost muscle.

mix_items.title: Chronic loneliness increases dementia risk by 38%, but occasional loneliness appears harmless, 30-year study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study that tracked people over the course of 30 years finds that only chronic, persistent loneliness is strongly linked with dementia.

mix_items.title: The Gulf's oil-eating microbes lay in wait before Deepwater Horizon spill, frozen samples suggest
mix_items.summary: A year before the Deepwater Horizon spill, a NOAA crew scooped up seawater from the Gulf and froze it. Sixteen years later, FIU biologist Shen Jean Lim tested it only to discover the microbes that devoured much of the oil in 2010 were nowhere to be found in 2009. So where did they come from?

mix_items.title: Forgetful neural networks could shed light on how humans learn
mix_items.summary: How the brain learns is one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in science. Researchers in artificial intelligence from the University of Groningen (the Netherlands) and KU Leuven (Belgium) hope that a specific type of forgetting in artificial neural networks will help to capture what is happening in the human brain. The study is published in the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

mix_items.title: Lasers near physical limits of miniaturization open possibilities for tracking life at the nanoscale
mix_items.summary: From tracking how cancer develops to exploring how the brain works, scientists need ways to observe biological processes at increasingly smaller scales. Beyond tracking how cells move and interact, researchers need to understand how tiny structures within cells, including organelles and molecular complexes, behave and change over time. However, identifying and tracking these microscopic targets individually remains a major challenge.

mix_items.title: New model identifies priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

mix_items.title: New daisy genus named after botanist
mix_items.summary: Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) botanist professor Pieter Pelser has been recognized with one of the highest honors in taxonomy, with a newly established South American daisy genus named Pelseria in acknowledgment of his decades-long contribution to studying the family tree of plants.

mix_items.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
mix_items.summary: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

mix_items.title: New Asian flying frog species identified in Indonesia
mix_items.summary: In the lush mountain rainforests of Indonesia, researchers have identified a new species of Asian flying frog with distinctive physical features, calls and unusual egg-laying habits. The discovery is described in a paper published in the journal Zootaxa by scientists from Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense in Indonesia, the University of California, Davis, and other collaborators.

mix_items.title: Regenerated bone keeps maturing after its shape is largely restored, study reveals
mix_items.summary: Regeneration is often judged by what researchers can see—whether missing tissue has returned and its shape has been restored. But a new Texas A&M study shows that bone may continue to mature mechanically beneath the surface even after it appears whole.

mix_items.title: Extreme cold preserves passion fruit's vitamin C, but not all of its antioxidants
mix_items.summary: Passion fruit can travel thousands of kilometers before it reaches international markets. Along the way, one of the food industry's biggest challenges is making sure its nutritional qualities survive processing, storage and transport.

mix_items.title: Optimized supercomputer workflow accelerates protein-structure prediction
mix_items.summary: A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)-led team has harnessed the power of El Capitan to accelerate generation of predicted protein structures, drastically reducing the computing time required and opening new possibilities for drug discovery, biological research and national security applications.

mix_items.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write […]

mix_items.title: Your gut bacteria help your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
mix_items.summary: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

mix_items.title: Repurposed battery molecules drive key chemical reactions where oil meets water
mix_items.summary: The process of producing essential medicines and fine chemicals has long been powered by reactions involving intense heat, heavy-metal catalysts and hazardous hydrogen gas. Now, a team of Harvard chemists and engineers has demonstrated that these critical transformations can be driven cleanly by electricity, right at the boundary where oil and water meet.

mix_items.title: Two proteins key to cellulose synthase trafficking and cell wall formation identified
mix_items.summary: A new study has identified Arabidopsis SNARE proteins VAMP726 and VAMP725 as key components of the trafficking of cellulose synthase (CESA), helping support the formation of both primary and secondary cell walls.

mix_items.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
mix_items.summary: On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% […]

mix_items.title: New platform improves accuracy of molecular counting in RNA-sequencing
mix_items.summary: The open-source platform, called UMIche (pronounced "you-me-kay"), is described in a new study published in Nature Communications. It addresses a common challenge in RNA-sequencing, where errors during sequencing can lead to inaccurate measurements of gene expression.

mix_items.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
mix_items.summary: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

mix_items.title: Novel algorithm predicts brain surgery outcomes in dystonia patients
mix_items.summary: Less than 5% of patients with dystonia—a debilitating neurological movement disorder—undergo deep brain stimulation (DBS) treatment, even though it is one of the few interventions that directly target the abnormal brain processes underlying the condition. The surgical treatment is highly underutilized, likely due to its invasiveness and the lack of objective markers of who may benefit. Even among those who undergo surgery, outcomes vary widely, depending on patient characteristics and external influences.

mix_items.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

mix_items.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

mix_items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
